text:
My first 3D graphics card was a 3dfx Voodoo3 3000 with 16MB from 1999. It runs at 166.66MHz, has 1 pixel pipeline with 2 texture mapping units (TMU). It's capable of a pixel fill rate of 166.66 megapixels/sec. and a texture fill rate of 333.33 megatexels/sec. It was frickin awesome back then.

Fast forward 25 years later and we have this arguably mid-range graphics card for ~$330 that boosts up to 2,655MHz with 64 ROPs (pixel pipes) and 128 TMUs. If you do the math it's about 1,020x faster in both pixel fill rate and texture fill rate, and it also has a thousand times more VRAM. 

I'd buy this if only to have the satisfaction of having a GPU that's a thousand times greater in every way than my first 3D graphics card. Well, except for the polygon performance. The 3dfx was supposedly good for 7 million triangles/sec. but no one really talks about polygon performance these days anymore, so I wonder how many triangles/sec. the Radeon 7600 XT is capable of.

text:
Three problems with this review, and I know that’s not what you want to read after sleeping in the office to get it out on time. 1. Your benchmarks focus on FPS performance and do not measure image quality in any way, which is a problem when games load lower quality (or fail to load) textures. This will lead you to discount the effects of adequate VRAm in your conclusions. 2. AMD systematically overstates their MSRPs, where Nvidia will gladly dry up their MSRP stock whenever they can consistently sell their commodity product above it. This leads reviewers to give Nvidia better reviews on average, even though they know AMD will discount their offerings for the majority of their lifetime. More specifically, AMD sets MSRPs they know all their AIBs can hit without special deals, where Nvidia typically only allows cards to hit MSRP in small numbers at launch, then continues to provide special subsidies only as necessary to move product. This allows AMD’s more efficient AIBs to sell cards below MSRP almost immediately, consistently creating a greater discrepancy between AMD and Nvidia pricing than MSRPs alone would suggest. I think the conclusions of AMD reviews that reject the cards for MSRP should say “well, if you can get it for $300 or less, it’s a good card,” for example, rather than blanket not recommending them. By telling your viewers you will revisit the card if it drops in price (and saying, “and it will,”) you are sacrificing AMD’s reputation to encourage your viewers to be dependent on you again at a later date, and potentially exposing your viewers to the risk of missing the best deals because they have to wait for your video examining said deals.
3. The conclusion of this video fails to provide an alternative GPU with more than 8 GB VRAM for a similar price, which people considering the 7600 XT might need to know. For anyone interested, the AMD 6700 XT and 6800 are good choices, offering more performance with adequate memory for not dissimilar prices right now.

TSMC 7nm - Ryzen 3000/5000, RX 5000/6000
TSMC 6nm - RX6500, RX7000, Intel Arc

Nvidia had the 8GB 128-bit PCie X8 4060 Ti, AMD had the 8GB 128-bit PCIe X8 7600.

It's PR - everyone pooped on Nvidia for the 8GB 4060 with a 128-bit bus. This is all the aftermath of that. 

It also has to do with the bus width - 12GB would use a faster 192-bit bus which is costlier to manufacture. People seriously underestimate the cost and engineering of basic I/O. 

Look at the 7800X3D de-lidded - the 8 cores of the fastest gaming CPU in the world is significantly smaller than it's I/O die which provides PCIe 5 and DDR5 connectivity.
author: @aminy23

text: @aminy23  The RTX4060 is already one of the smallest GPU's ever to have a 128bit bus being at only 158mm^2. I'm trying to look up it there was any GPU ever made with a sub 200mm^2 die and a 192bit bus but it doesn't seem like it.
author: @lharsay

text:
@lharsay  Correct - and that's exactly my point. The silicon needed for a 192-bit bus would have made it substantially larger and more expensive. 

The 1060 was exactly 200mm^2, and the 6GB version had a 192-bit bus. 

But 200mm^2 is over 25% larger - which is steep when attempting a budget card on a bleeding edge node. 

I/O is expensive and takes up silicon. Efficiency uses expensive nodes. 

The best performance for dollar comes with older nods where you don't have to cut features.

When RTX 40 came out, almost nothing used 4nm or better. This is super rare in the GPU market. The HD 7970 debuting TSMC 28nm in 2011 is the only example I can think of.

text:
It all has to do with node. If you use an expensive bleeding edge node - you get an expensive high performance GPU. If you use a cheap discount node, you get a value GPU with bad efficiency. 

As we move to expensive nodes, then you have to trim other features to keep in the price in check. For example AMD's Phoenix Ryzen 8000 desktop APUs use the TSMC 4nm node, so they cut PCIe 5.0 support, and they cut it to X4 for the first GPU slot, and X2 for the M.2 slot.

Likewise Nvidia's attempt to make a budget GPU with TSMC 4nm meant the 4060 had a 128 bit memory bus and reduced PCIe lanes as well.

The upcoming GPUs will be disappattmemptointments compared to bleeding edge predecessors, but their drop in price will be welcome. The launch day price is nonsense, eventually it will settle at a market price that's way different. 

TSMC 6nm is the sweet spot for value, and it's a shame to see to see the MSRP of this card.

@GamersNexus  Here are some specific benchmarks for running LLMs Locally.  The benchmarks are:  
1. Number of layers that can be offloaded to GPU using CLBlast (which is a function of VRAM)
2. Time it takes to process input prompt
3. Tokens generated per second
author: @adamsorrentino8233

text:
To measure these benchmarks, I propose the following steps
1. Download and setup LLM using the steps provided in “*Incredibly* simple guide to run language models locally on your PC, in 5 simple steps for non-techies.”
2. When Launching the LLM via Kobold, use Trial and error to offload as many layers of the LLM to the GPU as possible with the LLM still able to function (this will get benchmark for the number of layers)
3. Set the LLM's temperature to 0 to minimize randomness for testing.
4. Put in a specific testing prompt that is at (or slightly less than) the maximum size the LLM can accept (2k tokens)
5. Watch the LLM execute in the Kobold command window, and time how long it take to process the input to get Benchmark 2, and then the rate at which it generates tokens per second after it starts generating its reply.
6. Repeat these steps with different LLMs/different versions of the same LLM.

You can find additional LLMs with vastly different resource requirements at 
The origial Reddit page recommends guanaco-7B-GGML, Nous-Hermes-13B-GGML, and WizardLM-30B-GGML 
The Bloke has several versions of WizardLM at which have different quantizations, and vastly different performance and memory requirements.  The smallest 2 bit quantized one can fit in 16.1GB of RAM.
